questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code handles asynchronous execution (locking, background work, blocking calls)? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
Many coroutines call _lock_for for the same new provider at the same time. Why does the lazy creation of the lock not produce two different Lock objects?
choices: Dictionary reads and writes in Python acquire an internal lock that makes the whole method atomic across tasks.
There is no await between the lookup and the assignment, so no other task can run in between on the event loop.
asyncio.Lock instances are singletons per name, so a second creation returns the first.
The method is only called while the semaphore is held, which serializes callers.

questions.prompt: The SMTP server is down and send_confirmation raises after book() has already returned the appointment to its caller. What happens?
choices: The caller of book() receives the exception because the notification task is awaited before returning.
The exception is silently lost because the task object is garbage collected.
The appointment insert is rolled back because the lock context has already exited with an error.
The appointment stays booked; the done callback logs a warning and the failure does not reach the caller.

questions.prompt: book_many receives three requests for the same provider and the same start time, and the slot is initially free. What is the outcome?
choices: One request is booked and the other two end up in the failed list with SlotTaken.
All three are booked because the checks run concurrently before any insert.
The first failure cancels the remaining requests and book_many raises.
The calls deadlock because they contend for the same provider lock and the semaphore.
